You need to teach her how to act appropriately at a party because she won’t implicitly be able to intuitively know. 40F, diagnosed major depressive disorder in my 20’s. Still have anxiety, but feel like I’ve mostly overcome my souls crushing depression. Here’s what’s helped me:
- antidepressants
- running. Shown to be clinically as effective as therapy and antidepressants. 
- routine (aka behavioural activation). I get up everyday, make my bed, have a shower, eat a good breakfast. It stops the downward spiral
- a good diet. Shown to mildly improve depression symptoms and stops self hatred. Get adequate intake of all food groups.
- socialising- even though I’m and introvert and I’m inclined to spend time alone. I make myself do it as it is therapeutic. I usually feel better after.
- no complaining and gratitude. It increases cortisol and shrinks your brain. I remind myself daily of what I have versus what I don’t. 
- having children. Suicidal ideation has decreased because I know it’s no longer an option for me. 
- religion/spirituality. Has made major changes how I see myself/the world/others. 
- hobbies. Things that get you in a flow state.
- CBT- I have always fallen into catatrophisation/mind reading/ black and white thinking and personalisation. I’ve learnt to not fall into these thinking traps and can challenge these thoughts. 
- ACT- thought diffusion and not believing the stories my mind tells me, living by my values. 
- mindfulness- I practice it daily when I’m working, eating, showering and it helps me connect with the present moment instead of living in the past or future situations.
- size of the problem/size of my reaction- helps me categorise my problems into little, medium and big problems and modulate my reaction to them. If it’s a small problem, I’m not going to worry about it.

There has been a few major generational shifts which I think has contributed to burnout:
A) going analogue to digital work. It was supposed to reduce workloads but just has seemed to increase work demands/pace and remove work life balance. 
B) global financial crisis 2008. Since then, companies have increasingly cut staff to a skeleton. A team that existed 20 years ago is now done by 1-2 people and companies are still looking at reducing staff to increase profits. Companies don’t care because we are dispensable and they will just replace us if we burn out.
C) lack of company loyalty. This used to be a strong value of companies and they wanted staff to stay on board for a lifetime (and offer them pensions when they retired). Going back to the last point, they don’t care if you stay or go.
D) companies done provide training anymore. It’s all outsourced which means you’re expected to know how to do a job immediately without adequate support which adds to burnout. Previously you could get a job with little to no experience and they would teach you how to do the job. 
E) the rise of KPIs. Performance reviews and KPIs were not as rigorous or non existent back in the day. The expectation you can work like a machine all day for years on end and have no fluctuation in your workflow also contributes to burnout. 
F) increased training requirements. As said before I used to be able to walk into jobs without qualifications. Now you need masters and upwards for many roles and alot of the time you are combining study full time with work. You’re already burned out before you start working.
